case_name: F. N. Roy v Collector of Customs, Calcutta
respondent:
Collector of Customs, Calcutta
Supreme Court of India

16  May  1957
Petition No. 438 of 1955
The Judgment was delivered by : A. K. Sarkar, J.
1. By a notification dated March 16, 1953, the Government of India gave general permission to all persons to import into India from certain countries any goods of any of the descriptions specified in the schedule annexed to the notification. Among the goods specified in the Schedule were the following: Iron and steel chains of all sorts assessable under item 63 (28) of the Indian Customs Tariff, excluding chains for automobiles and cycles whether cut to length or in rolls. The petitioner is an importer of goods. He states that relying on the notification mentioned above he placed an order with a company in Japan sometime in August, 1953, for the supply of certain goods called in the trade, Zip Chains.

facts: The Government of India gave general permission to all persons to import into India from certain countries any goods of any of the descriptions specified in the schedule annexed to the notification.
The petitioner is an importer of goods and placed an order with a company in Japan for the supply of certain goods called Zip Chains.
The goods arrived in the port of Calcutta and the petitioner's bank paid the price of the goods amounting to Rs. 11,051-4-0.

Before the goods could be cleared from the port of Calcutta, the petitioner received a communication from the Assistant Collector of Customs for Appraisement, Calcutta, stating that it had been found that the petitioner did not possess valid import licence for the goods and requiring him to show cause why the goods should not be confiscated and action taken against the petitioner under s. 167, item 8, of the Sea Customs Act.
The communication also enquired if the petitioner wanted to be heard in person.

The petitioner submitted a written explanation stating that the Zip Chains imported by him were chains of the kind free import of which had been permitted by the notification of March 16, 1953, and therefore no licence to import them was necessary.
He was thereafter again asked by the Customs-authorities whether he wanted a personal hearing to which he replied that he did not.
Thereafter on December 25, 1953, the Collector of Customs made an order confiscating the goods and imposing a penalty of Rs. 1,000 on the petitioner.
This order bore an endorsement that it had been despatched to the petitioner on February 1, 1954.
The order stated that an appeal would lie against it to the Central Board of Revenue, New Delhi, within three months from the date of its despatch as noted on it.
The petitioner preferred an appeal and posted the memorandum of appeal on May 4, 1954.
The memorandum reached the Central Board of Revenue on May 6, 1954, and was dismissed on the ground that it had been preferred after the expiry of the time limited for the purpose.
The petitioner then made an application to the Government of India for revision of the order of the Central Board of Revenue but this application was rejected.

The petitioner thereafter applied to the High Court of Punjab under Art. 226 of the Constitution for an appropriate writ to quash the order confiscating his goods and imposing the fine on him but this application too was dismissed.
The petitioner has now applied to this Court under Art. 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order made against him.
issues: What is the effect of s. 3(2) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947 on s. 183 of the Sea Customs Act?
Is the order of confiscation made in this case bad because it did not give the petitioner an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation?
petitioner_arguments: The order of confiscation was bad because it did not give the petitioner an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.
S. 183 of the Sea Customs Act as modified by the Act of 1947 offends Art. 14 of the Constitution and therefore the order of confiscation is bad.

The portion of s. 3(2) of the Act of 1947 which read 'except that s. 183 thereof shall have effect as if for the word 'shall' therein the word 'may' were substituted' left an uncontrolled discretion in the Customs-authorities to give or not to give an option to pay a fine in lieu of compensation and consequently offended Art. 14 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The order of confiscation was not bad because it did not give the petitioner an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.
S. 183 of the Sea Customs Act as modified by the Act of 1947 does not offend Art. 14 of the Constitution and therefore the order of confiscation is valid.

The modification made by s. 3(2) of the Act of 1947 to s. 183 of the Sea Customs Act did not give any discretion to the Customs-authorities and therefore it did not offend Art. 14 of the Constitution.
court_reasoning: The order of confiscation was not bad because it did not give the petitioner an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.
S. 183 of the Sea Customs Act as modified by the Act of 1947 does not offend Art. 14 of the Constitution and therefore the order of confiscation is valid.

The modification made by s. 3(2) of the Act of 1947 to s. 183 of the Sea Customs Act did not give any discretion to the Customs-authorities and therefore it did not offend Art. 14 of the Constitution.
holding: The order of confiscation was valid and the petitioner's application under Art. 32 of the Constitution challenging its validity is dismissed.
